title: Chemistry — The particulate nature of matter
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: Chemistry — The particulate nature of matter, KS3 Science (National Curriculum).
meta_desc: KS3 Science practice covering Chemistry — The particulate nature of matter, from the National Curriculum programme of study.
final_note: You worked through Chemistry — The particulate nature of matter: 2 programme-of-study statements.

concepts.def: A scientific model in which all matter is made of huge numbers of tiny particles that are always moving. The particles are far too small to see, even with a microscope. Solid, liquid and gas forms of one substance contain the same particles: what is different is how the particles are arranged, how close together they are and how they move. The particles themselves do not change size, melt or boil, and the spaces between them are empty.
concepts.specStatementText: the properties of the different states of matter (solid, liquid and gas) in terms of the particle model, including gas pressure

concepts.def: A state of matter in which the particles are close together (touching), held in fixed places, usually in a regular pattern, and vibrate on the spot. Because the particles cannot move past each other, a solid has a fixed shape and a fixed volume, cannot flow, and can hardly be squashed.
concepts.specStatementText: the properties of the different states of matter (solid, liquid and gas) in terms of the particle model, including gas pressure

concepts.def: A state of matter in which the particles are close together (touching) but arranged randomly, with no pattern. They move around and slide past each other. So a liquid has a fixed volume but takes the shape of its container, can flow (be poured), and can hardly be squashed.
concepts.specStatementText: the properties of the different states of matter (solid, liquid and gas) in terms of the particle model, including gas pressure

concepts.def: A state of matter in which the particles are far apart, with empty space between them, arranged randomly and moving quickly in all directions. So a gas has no fixed shape or volume, spreads out to fill any container it is in, and can be squashed easily.
concepts.specStatementText: the properties of the different states of matter (solid, liquid and gas) in terms of the particle model, including gas pressure

concepts.def: To push a substance into a smaller volume. A gas can be compressed easily because there is a lot of empty space between its particles. Solids and liquids can hardly be compressed at all, because their particles are already touching.
concepts.specStatementText: the properties of the different states of matter (solid, liquid and gas) in terms of the particle model, including gas pressure

concepts.def: The push of a gas on the walls of its container. It is caused by the gas particles hitting the walls: each hit gives a tiny push, and huge numbers of hits every second add up to the pressure. A gas that is just sitting still in a container still has a pressure, because its particles are always moving.
concepts.specStatementText: the properties of the different states of matter (solid, liquid and gas) in terms of the particle model, including gas pressure

concepts.term: Heating a gas in a sealed container
concepts.def: If a gas is heated in a container that cannot get bigger, its particles move faster. They hit the walls harder and more often, so the pressure rises. The particles do not get bigger.
concepts.specStatementText: the properties of the different states of matter (solid, liquid and gas) in terms of the particle model, including gas pressure

concepts.def: If a gas is pushed into a smaller volume and kept at the same temperature, its particles are closer together and hit the walls more often, so the pressure rises. The particles themselves are not squashed.
concepts.specStatementText: the properties of the different states of matter (solid, liquid and gas) in terms of the particle model, including gas pressure

concepts.def: A change between solid, liquid and gas, such as melting or boiling. It is a physical change: no new substance is made, the particles stay the same and the mass stays the same. Only the arrangement, closeness and movement of the particles change. Energy is transferred to a substance to melt or boil it, and from it when it freezes or condenses.
concepts.specStatementText: changes of state in terms of the particle model

concepts.def: The change from solid to liquid. Energy is transferred to the solid; its particles vibrate faster until they break out of their fixed places and can move around each other. A pure substance melts at a fixed temperature, its melting point (ice melts at 0 °C).
concepts.specStatementText: changes of state in terms of the particle model

concepts.def: The change from liquid to solid. Energy is transferred from the liquid to its colder surroundings; its particles settle into fixed places, where they can only vibrate. A pure substance freezes at the same temperature as it melts.
concepts.specStatementText: changes of state in terms of the particle model

concepts.def: The change from liquid to gas that happens all through the liquid, at one temperature: the boiling point (100 °C for pure water at normal air pressure). Energy is transferred to the liquid, and bubbles of the substance's own gas form inside the liquid and rise.
concepts.specStatementText: changes of state in terms of the particle model

concepts.def: The change from liquid to gas that happens only at the surface of the liquid, and can happen at temperatures well below the boiling point. The fastest-moving particles at the surface escape into the air. Puddles and wet washing dry by evaporation.
concepts.specStatementText: changes of state in terms of the particle model

concepts.def: The change from gas to liquid. Energy is transferred from the gas, for example when it touches a cold surface; its particles come close together as a liquid. Water vapour in the air condenses into drops on a cold window or a cold can.
concepts.specStatementText: changes of state in terms of the particle model

concepts.def: The change from solid straight to gas, with no liquid in between. Particles break free from the solid and move apart as a gas. For example, solid carbon dioxide (dry ice) sublimes at room temperature.
concepts.specStatementText: changes of state in terms of the particle model

concepts.def: Water in the gas state. Like most gases it is invisible. The white cloud above a kettle and the mist on a cold morning are not water vapour: they are tiny drops of liquid water that have condensed from it.
concepts.specStatementText: changes of state in terms of the particle model

mcqs.q: Why does a solid, such as a block of iron, keep its own shape?
options: Its particles are too hard to bend
Its particles are not moving at all
Iron fills the gaps between its particles
Its particles are held in fixed places
mcqs.specStatementText: the properties of the different states of matter (solid, liquid and gas) in terms of the particle model, including gas pressure
mcqs.explain: Yes. Each particle is held in a fixed place, where it can only vibrate. The particles cannot move past each other, so the shape stays the same.
rationales: You may have thought the particles are hard because iron is hard. In fact a single particle does not have the properties of the solid; the shape stays fixed because the particles are held in fixed places.
You may have thought the particles in a solid are still because the solid looks still. In fact they vibrate all the time; they just stay in their fixed places.
You may have thought there must be more iron in the gaps between the particles. In fact the gaps are empty; the particles are all there is.
Yes. Each particle is held in a fixed place, where it can only vibrate. The particles cannot move past each other, so the shape stays the same.

mcqs.q: Which describes the particles in liquid water?
options: In neat rows, with small gaps between them
Close together, with more water filling the gaps
Touching, random, and sliding past each other
Soft and runny, so that each one can flow
mcqs.specStatementText: the properties of the different states of matter (solid, liquid and gas) in terms of the particle model, including gas pressure
mcqs.explain: Yes. In a liquid the particles are close together and touching, but in no pattern. They move around and slide past each other, which is why a liquid can be poured.
rationales: You may have pictured a liquid as a solid with a few gaps. In fact a liquid's particles are in no pattern, and they are touching, about as close as in the solid.
You may have thought there is water between the water particles. In fact the particles are the water; there is nothing between them.
Yes. In a liquid the particles are close together and touching, but in no pattern. They move around and slide past each other, which is why a liquid can be poured.
You may have thought the particles are runny because water is. In fact each particle stays the same; a liquid flows because its particles can slide past each other.

mcqs.q: The diagram shows the particles of a gas in a jar. Half of the gas is pumped out and the jar is sealed. Which describes the gas left in the jar?
options: Packed together at the bottom of the jar
Spread out evenly through the whole jar
Gathered near the top, as gas particles float
Spread out, with air filling the gaps
mcqs.specStatementText: the properties of the different states of matter (solid, liquid and gas) in terms of the particle model, including gas pressure
mcqs.explain: Yes. The particles move fast in all directions, so they still fill the whole jar. There are fewer of them, so they are further apart than before.
rationales: You may have thought gas particles settle at the bottom like a solid or a liquid. In fact they move fast in all directions and fill the whole jar.
Yes. The particles move fast in all directions, so they still fill the whole jar. There are fewer of them, so they are further apart than before.
You may have thought gas particles float because gases seem weightless. In fact they have mass, and they spread through the whole jar because they move fast in all directions.
You may have thought something must fill the space that was left. In fact the space between the particles is empty; nothing fills the gaps.

mcqs.q: What causes the pressure of the air inside a sealed bottle?
options: Air particles hitting all of the walls
Air particles pulling on one another
Air particles packed tight against the walls
Air particles floating up against the lid
mcqs.specStatementText: the properties of the different states of matter (solid, liquid and gas) in terms of the particle model, including gas pressure
mcqs.explain: Yes. The air particles move fast in all directions and keep hitting the walls. Each hit is a tiny push, and huge numbers of hits add up to the pressure.
rationales: Yes. The air particles move fast in all directions and keep hitting the walls. Each hit is a tiny push, and huge numbers of hits add up to the pressure.
You may have thought forces between the particles cause the pressure. In fact air particles are far apart; the pressure comes from them hitting the walls.
You may have thought the particles in air are packed closely together. In fact they are far apart, with empty space between them; the pressure comes from them hitting the walls.
You may have thought gas particles float to the top. In fact they move in all directions and hit every wall, not just the lid.

mcqs.q: The diagram shows gas particles in a strong, sealed metal container. The container warms up on a hot day. Why does the gas pressure rise?
options: The particles get bigger and push on the walls
The forces between the particles get stronger
Particles of heat get in and add to the gas
The particles hit the walls harder and more often
mcqs.specStatementText: the properties of the different states of matter (solid, liquid and gas) in terms of the particle model, including gas pressure
mcqs.explain: Yes. Warming makes the particles move faster. They hit the walls harder and more often, so the pressure rises.
rationales: You may have thought the particles swell when they are warmed. In fact each particle stays the same size; it is their speed that increases.
You may have thought forces between the particles cause the pressure. In fact the pressure comes from the particles hitting the walls, and warming makes the hits harder and more frequent.
You may have thought heat is a substance made of particles. In fact no new particles get into the sealed container; energy is transferred to the gas, so its particles move faster.
Yes. Warming makes the particles move faster. They hit the walls harder and more often, so the pressure rises.

mcqs.q: Air is sealed in a syringe. The plunger is pushed in and held still for a minute. Why is the air pressure now higher?
options: Its particles have been squashed smaller
Its particles hit the walls more often
Its particles are now touching each other
Its particles only push when it is squashed
mcqs.specStatementText: the properties of the different states of matter (solid, liquid and gas) in terms of the particle model, including gas pressure
mcqs.explain: Yes. The same particles are now in a smaller space, so they reach the walls and hit them more often. More hits each second means a higher pressure.
rationales: You may have thought squashing the air squashes each particle. In fact the particles stay the same size; they are just closer together.
Yes. The same particles are now in a smaller space, so they reach the walls and hit them more often. More hits each second means a higher pressure.
You may have thought the particles in a squashed gas are pressed together. In fact they are still far apart; they hit the walls more often because the space is smaller.
You may have thought air only pushes on the walls while it is being squashed. In fact its particles were hitting the walls before you pushed; now they hit them more often.

mcqs.q: A sealed syringe of air can be pushed in a long way. The same syringe filled with water hardly moves. Why?
options: Water particles have water in the gaps
Air particles are soft and squash easily
Air particles have large spaces between them
Air particles are lighter than water ones
mcqs.specStatementText: the properties of the different states of matter (solid, liquid and gas) in terms of the particle model, including gas pressure
mcqs.explain: Yes. In air the particles are far apart, so pushing moves them closer together. In water the particles are already touching, so there is almost no space to squash them into.
rationales: You may have thought there is water between the water particles. In fact the gaps are empty; water cannot be squashed because its particles are already touching.
You may have thought air particles are squashy because air is. In fact the particles do not change size; air can be squashed because of the large spaces between them.
Yes. In air the particles are far apart, so pushing moves them closer together. In water the particles are already touching, so there is almost no space to squash them into.
You may have thought gases are squashable because they are light. In fact how heavy the particles are does not matter here; what matters is the space between them.

mcqs.q: The diagram shows the particles of a substance before and after it melts. What happens to the particles as it melts?
options: They leave fixed places and move around
They melt and turn into tiny drops of liquid
They dissolve and turn the solid into a solution
They start to move, as before they were still
mcqs.specStatementText: changes of state in terms of the particle model
mcqs.explain: Yes. Energy makes the particles vibrate faster until they break out of their fixed places. In the liquid they move around and slide past each other.
rationales: Yes. Energy makes the particles vibrate faster until they break out of their fixed places. In the liquid they move around and slide past each other.
You may have thought the particles melt along with the solid. In fact the particles stay exactly the same; only how they are arranged and how they move changes.
You may have thought melting and dissolving are the same. In fact dissolving needs a second substance to dissolve in; here one substance changes from solid to liquid.
You may have thought the particles in a solid do not move. In fact they were already vibrating; melting lets them move out of their fixed places.

mcqs.q: Pure water has been boiling in a beaker for ten minutes. Big bubbles keep forming inside the water. What is in the bubbles?
options: Air that was mixed into the water
Water that has turned into a gas
Hydrogen and oxygen from split water
Heat that is escaping from the hot water
mcqs.specStatementText: changes of state in terms of the particle model
mcqs.explain: Yes. Boiling happens all through the liquid: water particles break away inside it and form bubbles of water vapour, which rise and escape.
rationales: You may have thought the bubbles are air. Small bubbles of air do appear when water is first warmed, but after ten minutes of boiling the big bubbles are water vapour.
Yes. Boiling happens all through the liquid: water particles break away inside it and form bubbles of water vapour, which rise and escape.
You may have thought boiling splits water into hydrogen and oxygen. In fact boiling is a change of state; the water particles stay as water particles.
You may have thought heat is a substance that can fill bubbles. In fact heating transfers energy, which is not a gas; the bubbles contain water vapour.

mcqs.q: A thin layer of water is left on a glass plate. A day later the plate is dry. What happened to the water particles?
options: They only left once the water had boiled
They were used up and no longer exist
They escaped from the surface into the air
They soaked down into the plate itself
mcqs.specStatementText: changes of state in terms of the particle model
mcqs.explain: Yes. The fastest-moving particles at the surface of the water escaped into the air as a gas. This is evaporation, and it happens well below 100 °C.
rationales: You may have thought water must boil before it can turn into a gas. In fact water evaporates at room temperature; particles escape from its surface without boiling.
You may have thought the water has disappeared because you cannot see it. In fact its particles still exist; they are spread out in the air as water vapour.
Yes. The fastest-moving particles at the surface of the water escaped into the air as a gas. This is evaporation, and it happens well below 100 °C.
You may have thought the water soaked into the plate. In fact glass does not soak up water; the particles escaped into the air.

mcqs.q: The diagram shows a can of drink just out of a fridge. Drops of water form on the outside. Where does this water come from?
options: Drink seeping out through the metal
Coldness from the can turning into water
Hydrogen and oxygen gases joining together
Water vapour in the air that condenses
mcqs.specStatementText: changes of state in terms of the particle model
mcqs.explain: Yes. The air contains water vapour. When it touches the cold can it cools and condenses: its particles come close together as drops of liquid water.
rationales: You may have thought the drink leaks through the can. In fact the metal does not let the drink through; the water comes from water vapour in the air.
You may have thought cold is a thing that can flow out and become water. In fact cold is not a substance; the can takes energy from the water vapour in the air, which condenses.
You may have thought hydrogen and oxygen join to make the water. In fact this is a change of state, not a reaction: water vapour that was already in the air condenses.
Yes. The air contains water vapour. When it touches the cold can it cools and condenses: its particles come close together as drops of liquid water.

mcqs.q: Water boils in a kettle. Just above the spout is a clear gap, then a white cloud. What is the white cloud?
options: Tiny drops of liquid water
Water vapour, which is a gas
Heat you can see in the air
Hydrogen and oxygen gases
mcqs.specStatementText: changes of state in terms of the particle model
mcqs.explain: Yes. The clear gap is water vapour, a gas you cannot see. As it cools in the air it condenses into tiny drops of liquid water, which you can see.
rationales: Yes. The clear gap is water vapour, a gas you cannot see. As it cools in the air it condenses into tiny drops of liquid water, which you can see.
You may have thought the cloud is water vapour because it is called steam. In fact water vapour is invisible: it is the clear gap; the cloud is drops that have condensed.
You may have thought heat is a substance that you can see. In fact heat is energy being transferred, and it cannot be seen; the white cloud is tiny drops of water that have condensed.
You may have thought boiling splits water into hydrogen and oxygen. In fact water stays as water; the cloud is water that has condensed back into drops.

mcqs.q: A tray of water is put in a freezer and turns to ice. What happens during freezing?
options: Cold flows from the freezer into the water
All of the particles stop moving completely
Each particle freezes into a bit of ice
The water transfers energy to its surroundings
mcqs.specStatementText: changes of state in terms of the particle model
mcqs.explain: Yes. The freezer is colder than the water, so energy is transferred from the water to the freezer. Its particles settle into fixed places, where they still vibrate.
rationales: You may have thought cold is something that flows into things. In fact nothing called cold moves; energy moves out of the water into the colder freezer.
You may have thought particles in a solid are still. In fact in ice the particles still vibrate; they just stay in fixed places.
You may have thought the particles freeze along with the water. In fact each particle stays the same; only their arrangement and movement change.
Yes. The freezer is colder than the water, so energy is transferred from the water to the freezer. Its particles settle into fixed places, where they still vibrate.

mcqs.q: Dry ice is solid carbon dioxide. At room temperature it turns straight into a gas. What happens to its particles?
options: They each swell up into bigger particles
They break free and spread far and wide
They lose their weight and float away
They are used up and stop existing
mcqs.specStatementText: changes of state in terms of the particle model
mcqs.explain: Yes. This is sublimation. The particles break free from the solid and spread far apart as a gas, without becoming a liquid first.
rationales: You may have thought gas particles are bigger than solid ones. In fact the particles stay the same size; they are just much further apart in the gas.
Yes. This is sublimation. The particles break free from the solid and spread far apart as a gas, without becoming a liquid first.
You may have thought a gas has no weight. In fact every particle keeps its mass; gas particles spread out because they move fast in all directions, not because they float.
You may have thought the dry ice disappears because you cannot see the gas. In fact every particle still exists, spread out in the air as carbon dioxide gas.

specSource: National Curriculum in England, key stage 3 science — Chemistry; Chemistry — The particulate nature of matter (DfE 2013 programme of study, verbatim)

specStatements.text: the properties of the different states of matter (solid, liquid and gas) in terms of the particle model, including gas pressure
changes of state in terms of the particle model

scopeNotes.decision: The arrangement, closeness and movement of particles in solids, liquids and gases are used to explain shape, volume, how easily each state can be squashed (compressed) and whether it can flow; gas pressure is explained as gas particles hitting the walls of the container, and its rise when a gas is heated (faster particles) or squashed into a smaller volume (more frequent hits) is treated qualitatively; the particles themselves never expand, melt or change.
scopeNotes.basis: The chemistry statement asks only for properties 'in terms of the particle model, including gas pressure'. Pressure as force over area and density belong to the key stage 3 Physics headings 'Pressure in fluids' and 'Matter', and Brownian motion is listed there under 'Physical changes'. Calculations with density, pressure × volume = constant and kinetic energy are GCSE physics content (DfE, GCSE subject content for biology, chemistry and physics, 2015).
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No item, concept, misconception or rationale contains a calculation, a pressure or density value, a formula such as p = F/A or pV = constant, or a kinetic energy equation, and none mentions Brownian motion. Every pressure item asks only why the pressure rises or what causes it, in words. No key, concept, key rationale or misconception correction says or implies that particles themselves expand, shrink, melt or boil; that idea appears only in distractors and misconceptions, where it is corrected.

scopeNotes.decision: Melting, freezing, boiling, evaporating, condensing and sublimation are explained by changes in the arrangement and movement of the same particles; energy is said to be transferred to a substance to melt or boil it and from it when it freezes or condenses, without amounts; evaporation happens at the surface below the boiling point, and boiling happens all through the liquid.
scopeNotes.basis: The statement asks for 'changes of state in terms of the particle model'. Specific heat capacity, specific latent heat and their calculations are GCSE physics content (DfE, GCSE subject content for biology, chemistry and physics, 2015). The key stage 3 Physics heading 'Particle model' names 'the anomaly of ice-water transition', so particles moving further apart on melting is not stated as a rule.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No item, concept or rationale gives an amount of energy, a specific or latent heat, or a value read from a heating or cooling curve; the only temperatures used are the boiling point of water (100 °C) and the melting point of ice (0 °C). No item or rationale says that particles always move further apart when a solid melts.
